title: The encryption was never broken. Heartbleed was a missing length check, not a cracked cipher.
description:
Heartbleed was a missing length check, not a cracked cipher. The researchers called it a programming mistake in OpenSSL, not a flaw in the protocol.

Wrote the heartbeat feature and later said he missed validating a variable containing a length. A reviewer missed it too, and it was committed on 31 December 2011.

How much of a server's memory one malformed heartbeat request could read back. An attacker could simply ask again.

The flawed code shipped by default in March 2012 and was disclosed in April 2014. About 17% of trusted secure web servers were thought to be vulnerable.

Google's Neel Mehta and the security firm Codenomicon found it independently. Mehta reported it to OpenSSL on 1 April 2014. The fix, version 1.0.1g, came on 7 April.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heartbleed (read): established that Robin Seggelmann wrote the heartbeat extension in 2011 and later said he missed validating a variable containing a length; that Stephen Henson reviewed it and committed it on 31 December 2011; that heartbeat support shipped enabled by default in OpenSSL 1.0.1 on 14 March 2012; that Neel Mehta of Google privately reported it on 1 April 2014; that it was disclosed on 7 April 2014 with OpenSSL 1.0.1g; that about 17% of trusted secure web servers were believed vulnerable at disclosure; and that about 900 Canadian social insurance numbers were taken from the Canada Revenue Agency on 8 April 2014.
- https://heartbleed.com/ (read): the researchers' own page; established that the flaw was an implementation problem, a programming mistake in OpenSSL, and not a flaw in the protocol; that OpenSSL 1.0.1 to 1.0.1f were vulnerable; that each heartbeat could read 64 KB but the attacker could repeat requests; that Codenomicon and Neel Mehta found it independently; and that private keys, passwords and messages could be exposed.
